resources.string: Welcome to Matrix Method: 5k training program! Whether you\'re an experienced runner or just getting into it, there\'s something here for everyone.
For the best possible experience, read these tips carefully. With professional guidance, you really can get more out of every workout.

You\'ll begin with an assessment to gauge your experience as a runner. This assessment will consist of a five-minute warmup, 15-minute pace, and a five-minute cooldown. This assessment\'s speed will be controlled by you. It\'s important to try your hardest during this time, as you\'ll use the results as a baseline.
Throughout this assessment, be sure to challenge yourself while maintaining proper form and safety.
You\'re halfway there — keep pushing!
Only four minutes left — keep it up!
Amazing job! You\'ve completed the assessment portion and taken the first step toward becoming a 5k runner! Now you\'ll use your results to create a program tailored to your abilities.
Take the remaining few minutes to cool down, catch your breath and hydrate! It\'s critical to continue walking during cooldown periods to maximize the benefits to your health.
You\'ll begin today\'s workout with a long, slow distance run. The goal of this type of run is to increase endurance, increase blood volume, and help your body adapt to longer periods on your feet.
This type of run is generally done at a jogging pace. This will help keep you consistent and better adapt your body to long periods of running.

You\'re entering Zone 1. This is a low-intensity pace great for warming up and cooling down. Zones will be used throughout the eight weeks to give you an idea of the intensity you should be running at.
You\'re entering Zone 3. This zone is generally done at a jogging pace and can begin to feel slightly uncomfortable. Zone 3 helps with blood circulation and is where lactic acid begins to accumulate.

You\'re entering Zone 2. Zone 2 is a light intensity that can be done for a long period of time. This is a great zone for building general endurance, fighting fatigue, burning fat, and increasing muscular fitness.
Your intensity will make a difference in this program. Push yourself, and let\'s find out how far you can go.
You\'re doing awesome! Remember to continue to breathe and try to find a rhythm that works for you. This will make future runs much more manageable.
Great job, just one minute left! Use the last five minutes to cool down and reflect on how you did.
As you continue on this journey, it\'s important to remember to eat well, stay hydrated, replace your electrolytes, reduce stress, and get sufficient sleep.
Today, you\'ll be doing an Interval run. Interval runs involve deliberately changing your pace to incorporate high-intensity exercise with active recovery.
The goal for this run is to truly push yourself for one minute and take the two-minute walking breaks to recover as best as you can.
Remember, this is going to be difficult for a short period of time. However, this is going to get your body used to intense running conditions.

You\'re entering Zone 4. Zone 4 is where running gets hard, and your body is working close to its max. This zone helps with speed, endurance, and training your body to withstand high levels of lactic acid.
You\'ve hit the halfway point! Keep up the pace and continue pushing. Remember to focus on proper form throughout your run.
You\'re entering Zone 5. Zone 5 should push your body to its limit. This zone isn\'t sustainable over a longer period, but it\'s great for getting your body used to high-intensity workouts.
Amazing job! You\'ve pushed your body to its limits and worked extremely hard. Throughout these next eight weeks, you\'ll feel like some of these workouts become easier.
Continue to walk it out — recovery is an essential aspect of training.
The final workout for this week is going to be a tempo run. Tempo runs are long, sustained periods of running with short jogging breaks in between.
Tempo runs are often described as \'comfortably hard.\' You should be at a pace that you can do for a longer period of time. Think about being close to the pace you\'ll be running come race day.
As we begin, remember to push yourself and find a comfortably hard pace. You\'ll want to find a pace that you can sustain over a longer period of time.
You\'re almost halfway! I hope you\'ve found a good pace. Remember to keep your chin up, you\'re doing great.
Jog it out, you\'re almost done!

Great job this week. You have completed the first week of an eight-week journey, and you\'re one step closer to becoming a successful 5k runner. Remember, there will be points in your journey when you may doubt yourself, but you can do it!
Congratulations on this big step! You\'ll go even farther next week.
Welcome back to week 2. You\'re starting with a distance run again, and you\'re striving for balance on this run. Run at a good pace to get your blood pumping and get used to being on your feet.
This week you\'ll be adding an extra set to the distance run. This means you\'ll be running an extra four minutes with a one-minute break.
Keeping your chin up will help keep your shoulders back and your core firm. This is considered proper running form and will make your workout as efficient as possible.
We must make the investment in fitness because you never know when that fitness is going to pay off.
Your feet should always be positioned close to your center of gravity. By doing this, you keep yourself balanced and in control.
The goal is to land quickly and quietly.
If you\'re having a tough time visualizing the positioning of your hands, imagine holding fluttering butterflies to keep your hands soft.
Your hands should be up high on your torso, not down.

Are you struggling to understand what sort of running form you should be in? Think about running between two buildings that are very close together, just wide enough for you to get through the middle.
Great job today! You increased the distance of your run, and you made it look easy.
Continue to build good habits, especially when it comes to running form.
You may notice the interval run this week is harder than last week. Throughout this program, each week will get progressively harder than the last.
You need to be willing to push yourself to new limits if you want to see what you can truly achieve.
The more steps you take, the more efficient you can be.
If you do one mile and focus on doing nine perfect one-mile segments, you\'ll become a better runner.
You could get bitter, you could get angry, or you could get busy. So get busy!
Run tall, chin up, shoulders back.
You should always land with a slight bend in your knee.
When the workout seems too hard, think about what life will be like 20 or 30 years from now. Our current actions impact us significantly in the future.
This was another tough workout, but you pulled through. Look forward to the progress you\'ll make over these next six weeks as a runner and as a person.
You\'ve made it to the final workout for week 2. You\'ll be doing a tempo run that will last for approximately 30 minutes. Remember, tempo runs are supposed to be about 80–90% of your race pace.
Tempo runs are great for increasing your lactate-threshold pace. This type of run will directly benefit your ability to run for a longer period of time.
When you fall short, don’t become paralyzed by that. There\'s no need to fall into a quagmire of hopelessness and despair!
Don\'t forget the main reason you started running. Use that as your motivation!
You don\'t need to be a world-class athlete to be healthy. You just need to be consistent.
Whenever there is abundance in our lives, there tends to be waste and a lack of gratitude. Avoid this mindset at all costs!
Your chin should always be up — in running and in life!
Fantastic job! You had a great week, and you should be proud of the vast improvements in your running.
Make sure you\'re doing some dynamic stretching before each run. This will help you loosen up and reduce the chances of injury.
Welcome back to week 3. You\'re back to distance running today. Throughout this workout, try to focus on getting into a pattern with your breathing. This will help you run longer.
For distance runs, remember that you don\'t want to run too quickly. The goal of this run is to get you acclimated to being on your feet for an extended period of time.
You don\'t need to be a world-class athlete to be healthy, you just need to be consistent.
Variety is the spice of life, especially as an athlete.
Our true strength tends to lay dormant when we live lives of comfort and convenience.
Two things are true about positivity — when you see it, you know it, and when you have it, you feel it.
Remember to be disciplined with your pre-run dynamic movements. That will pay significant dividends over your lifetime.
You have to dig deep to accept a difficult situation. You also have to dig deep to make the best of that bad situation. But guess what? You can do it.
Great job getting through this run! This was close to a 45-minute workout, which is no small feat. Give yourself some praise and make sure to participate in active recovery.
Today, you\'re back with another interval run. I want to stress the importance of properly warming up before running. Interval runs are particularly stressful on your body.
Keeping yourself hydrated and in good form will be critical to a successful workout today.
Your internal embers can ignite into a raging fire of strength and determination during the darkness of tragedy.
There\'s nothing stronger, more compelling, or more beautiful than the human spirit. Especially when it\'s tested.
The reality is, by taking more steps or increasing your cadence, you\'re keeping better balance.
Remember to watch your pace and your breathing, and bring it down to a jog if needed.
We show our true selves when put to the test. Next time you think about quitting, remember why you started running to begin with.
Great job today! You may not be able to see it, but these interval runs are improving your cardiovascular health and overall fitness.

Hopefully you\'re warmed up and ready for today\'s tempo run. You\'ll be running an extra set today for a total time of around 36 minutes. Make sure to stay hydrated and focus on good form. Let\'s see what you can do!
Think about the type of pace you could run for an hour. At this type of pace, you\'ll be able to get an idea of how much more you can push your body come race day.
The comeback is always sweeter than the setback.
Always remember — never take anything or anyone for granted!
When you\'re running, one of the things you can do is take a walk break and walk backward. This can help with balance, coordination, and using different muscle groups.
You should base your workouts on your morning resting heart rate.
Incredible job today! You\'ve just completed the third week and are making some serious progress to becoming 5K ready. You should be extremely proud of what you\'ve accomplished so far.
Consider doing some light static stretching to finish your workout. This can help speed muscle recovery and ease feelings of soreness.
Welcome to week 4, the halfway point! This week, you\'ll continue to increase the distance and intensity of your workouts. This starts today with a distance run.
For today\'s run, focus on keeping good form. Shoulders should be back, chin should be up, core should be firm, and you want to be landing quickly but softly on your feet.
When running, try to land with your feet as close to your body as possible. This will help you take more steps and keep you balanced.
It\'s a good idea to begin with a pre-run dynamic movement segment of 5–10 minutes. This can include side lunges, high knees, glute kicks or lateral shuffles.
There\'s always a fight inside of you. You just have to have the will to step up and fight when you need it the most.
Long slow distance will help promote an efficient form of running.
We all have the power to be positive, because ultimately, it\'s our choice.
Whenever we have an abundance of anything, we tend to take it for granted until we lose it. Don\'t let this happen to you!
Awesome job today! Now, think back to your first distance run. Can you feel the difference? Just imagine where you\'ll be in four weeks! Keep up the great work!
Your heart is getting stronger! You\'re pumping more blood and metabolizing more oxygen, making your heart slightly more efficient every time you run.

You\'re kicking off today with another interval run. The run today will be pretty intense. You\'ll take on four one-minute intervals of straight sprinting. This will push your body intensely, so let\'s make sure you\'re ready.
Make sure you\'re warming up properly for every run, especially on interval days. Whether it\'s stretching or walking, you should be loose and flexible.
Our attitude is the one thing we have total control over.
Did you know? Studies have shown that running intervals at an anaerobic pace you can increase muscle mass.
You have everything it will take to be positive. But it\'s going to take everything you have to do it.
Fitness leads to positivity, and the combination of both leads to a great state of mental health.
If you keep fighting, and keep pushing forward. You will achieve your goals!
Make sure you are giving your body enough time to recover properly.
Another amazing workout! Remember to embrace the walking breaks. They\'re not just for recovery; they also provide a wide range of benefits to your body.
Get pumped for the last workout of this week! As you might have guessed, you\'re doing a tempo run.
You should be a pro at these by now. Remember that you want this run to be comfortably hard, and think about how you\'ll be running on race day.
Tough situations in your life have the ability to shape you into the person you want to be, so embrace challenge!
Running is just the simple act of balancing on one leg.
Remember, tempo runs will be challenging, but this practice will make you a more efficient runner.
Make sure to focus on your breathing, and practice getting into a rhythm. This is critical to succeeding in any long-form running.
Pushing yourself is how you grow, it\'s how you become a better runner, and it\'s how you improve overall.
A great stretching technique is to take a resistance band and put it around your ankles while doing half-moons.

What a way to end week 4! You\'ve made a lot of progress, and you should be starting to get a sense of ease when coming to these workouts. You\'re making real strides, and you\'re halfway to the finish line.
You\'re starting off week 5 strong. You have a distance run today, the longest one yet! You\'ll be going for close to 53 minutes, so as usual, stay hydrated, keep a good form and have fun.

Diet is an important part of distance running. You\'ll want to make sure you\'re loading up on carbs, as this will provide your body with glycogen which is essential for energy. You\'ll also want to have a healthy amount of protein for recovery.
Did you know? Studies have shown that running places 3–4 times your body weight on your legs with every foot strike. Having proper footwear is essential to reducing this impact.
Long slow distance is great for strengthening the muscles in your legs.
For proper form, imagine running like a 90-year-old person on a frozen lake.
Long slow distance runs will also burn a great amount of calories without being overly strenuous.
Repetitive impact is why more than 50% of runners experience some form of injury annually. One way to help reduce this risk is to shorten your stride and stretch regularly.
That was a long run, but you made it look easy! After completing that, you can be confident that in just a few weeks, you\'ll be 5k-ready.
It\'s important to consider what your diet is going to look like leading up to race day.
You\'re starting off this workout with interval runs. You should understand what to expect with these runs by now, and how each week you\'re going to push a little harder and go a little farther.
As always, make sure you\'re loose and flexible before starting this section. Take breaks if you need to, and stay hydrated!
Technology can be useful and provide data to gauge and improve your fitness journey. However, don\'t let it distract from your running form and rhythmic breathing!
Injuries can be minimized and prevented by practicing proper form.
Studies show that doing a short fifteen to thirty-minute High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) workout had the same health benefits as longer moderate exercise.
To maintain good form, you want your hands to remain soft and held close to your torso without crossing the center line.
It\'s important to make sure we are easing our way into these interval runs. There can be a lot of stress put on your joints, so taking time to recover is crucial.
You should aim to have your hips relaxed with minimal rotation. This will keep you in good form and minimize the risk of injury.
Finishing out the run very strong! Great job today!
You\'re back at it today with another tempo run. This time, you\'re looking at four sets of seven-minute runs, with two-minute jogs in between.
Remember to focus on keeping a strong form, patterning your breathing, and staying hydrated.
If you feel you\'re struggling with mental health, I hope you get comfortable being uncomfortable and share it with someone you love. Don’t be afraid of it.
The goal of a tempo run is to build up your speed and get you comfortable with running faster for a longer time.
Try landing your feet beneath your hips. This will keep you in good form.
By pushing yourself through these tempo runs, you\'re going to increase your race day speed drastically!
Try and visualize the surface you are running on as coming up to meet your feet and not the other way around.
A few pointers to help you keep form: always keep your chin up, your shoulders relaxed, your core firm, and your back straight.
It\'s always a great idea to continue your training, even when you\'re done with your session.
Focusing on mobility drills, strength training, and getting enough rest will create a successful and balanced schedule.
Welcome to week 6! You\'re quickly closing in on race week, and you\'re making fantastic progress.
You\'ll be going back to a distance run today. You\'re running for even longer this week, so this is a fantastic opportunity to get comfortable pacing yourself.
Take regular walk breaks to maintain efficient running form.
You\'re currently training your respiratory, cardio, and muscular system to be more efficient.
Rhythmic breathing can help you conserve your energy.
The ideal cadence is 165–180 steps per minute. Try to achieve 41–45 steps per 30-second segments to match this recommended cadence.
This run will not only help you burn more calories, but it is critical in helping your body adjust to running.
Run in the moment and be mindful of your form and breathing pattern throughout every workout.
Amazing job finishing this run! Being able to control your pace and manage the state you\'re in is critical for 5ks.

Today, you\'re taking on another interval run. This interval run is going to be intense, so when it gets tough, remember how far you\'ve come since starting out. Think about why you\'re running and why you want to complete a 5k, and use that to motivate yourself.
It\'s going to be important to focus on your breathing and using those walking breaks in between sprints. As always, if you\'re overextending yourself, take it down a notch.

There\'s a root cause for pain, and it\'s typically an imbalance or weakness somewhere in the kinetic chain. So, if you have a tight left Achilles, it\'s because of a weak right glute on the opposite side of your body. (the importance of post workout recovery)
High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) is a fantastic way to increase speed and decrease time for a 5k.
Running in these short bursts is great for Human Growth Hormone production, also known as hGH. hGH is responsible for health benefits like maintaining body structure, metabolism, and glucose levels.
Consider strength training on your off days. This can really help build the muscles in your legs.
HIIT has been shown to improve anaerobic and aerobic activities.
Improving mobility, stability, flexibility, and balance is key to becoming a better runner.
What an impressive run you just completed! Take these next few minutes to walk it off and cool down. You put in hard work today, and you should be proud.
You\'re at the last workout for week 6, and it\'s a tempo run. Make sure to watch your breathing and maintain good form.

Regularly monitoring your morning resting heat rate establishes a baseline for determining how well rested or how stressed your body is. This can help dictate the volume and intensity of your upcoming workout.
The two most important things for an athlete are hydration and sleep.
One aspect of running that gets overlooked is the mental challenge. Tempo runs are a great way to get used to this mental challenge and train yourself to overcome it.
If you want a benchmark on how much fluid you should drink per day, take your body weight and divide it in half. That\'s how many ounces you should be drinking.
Throughout this run, you\'ll want to be right below the pace you plan to be at on race day.
The more movement variety you can have, the more fit you\'re going to be.

Every night before you go to bed, elevate your legs. Do ankle rotations in different directions. Do a series of those, and then do Achilles stretches. This will benefit many different parts of your feet.
Fantastic job! That was a long run, and you got through it. You\'re almost ready to complete a 5k!
Welcome to week 7! This is going to be your toughest week of the program, but you can do it. You\'ve come a long way from week 1, and it\'s time to prove yourself.
You\'ll start with another distance run, so use everything you\'ve learned so far to your advantage. While this is your longest run of the program, you should be feeling confident and capable.
The biggest mistake that most runners make is that their first mile is their fastest mile.
The LSD will improve your ability to handle discomfort and allow you to become a more patient and disciplined runner.
Make sure to constantly control your pace. This will help your stamina and keep you focused.
Make sure you are staying hydrated. Being dehydrated can hinder your workout and make you more prone to injury.

Water should be your main source of hydration after these workouts. Studies show that unless you are engaged in high-intensity exercise for an extended period of time, the disadvantages outweigh the benefits.
Your first mile should be 60–90 seconds slower than you expect to average for the remaining miles.
Intense exercise will help increase the size of mitochondria and, in turn, improve the use of oxygen and glycogen storage.
It\'s important to focus on maintaining efficient form and breathing.
Fantastic job! You\'ve really proven that you\'re capable of so much. This was not an easy run by any means, so be proud.
You\'re back at the interval run. Remember your pre-run stretching and to focus on your form.
Your body and your heart especially need time to pump oxygen-rich blood to oxygenate your muscles.
Take regular walk breaks.
Your metabolic rate remains elevated for up to two hours after completing an interval exercise, extending the period for calorie burning.
Never run farther than a mile without taking a walk break.
While endurance training is generally done through long-form running, HIIT is a great way to improve oxygen consumption.
Pairing oatmeal with some fruit is a great breakfast before a 5k.
Great job! You\'re flying through these runs.
This tempo run is going to be the closest practice you have to a real 5k. Use this time to get comfortable running for a longer period at a sustained pace.
When it gets tough, don\'t let your mind wander into a place of doubt.
When lactic acid builds up in your muscles, it leads to fatigue. Tempo runs are a fantastic way to build up your tolerance against lactic acid and help you run faster for longer.
When you go for a run, never imagine going for a nine-mile run. Instead, imagine going for a one-mile run nine times.
Metrics are really important if you\'re tracking for improvement. Track your average pace, track your average heart rate, and track your cadence.
Make sure you\'re properly fueled, well-hydrated, and properly rested. These are vital components to running a good race.
The first 10 minutes of every workout should be an easy-to-moderate effort to allow your cardiovascular system and muscles to acclimate to the rigors of the workout.
Amazing job! You nailed week 7 and only have a few more workouts until you tackle your 5k.
Welcome to week 8, the final week! You\'ve made amazing progress over the past 7 weeks, and now it\'s time to put all that hard work together.
Week 8 is slightly different from the rest of the program in that it\'s not progressively harder than week 7. You should have enough energy at the end of this week to be able to complete a 5k.
It\'s always advisable to begin your workout with a dynamic movement warmup.
Make sure to complete a thorough post-workout cooldown.
You may be feeling tired right now, and that\'s ok, but try to continue to push yourself for as long as you can.
Stretch and foam roll your hips, glutes, and legs thoroughly.
Training often will adapt your ligaments, tendons, bones, and joints to the stressors of running.
Aim to sustain a consistent pace throughout the run.
Remember that your tempo runs should be anywhere from 70–80% of your maximum intensity.
Congratulations! That was the last distance run of the program. You are so close to your 5k.
After all these weeks of hard work, this Interval run should be a piece of cake!
Make sure you\'re looking ahead, keeping your hands near your waist, and not bouncing.
Making sure you\'re training lightly on your active recovery days is important. Don\'t skip this step!
The perfect post-workout drink just may be chocolate milk!
Although the interval workouts are generally short, they\'re an excellent way to lose weight.
Remember to refuel and hydrate within the first 30 minutes after every workout.
Consider foam rolling as a form of recovery. This will help relax your muscles and reduce soreness.
Sleeping more and sleeping better is a critical aspect of recovery.
What a great run today! You\'re looking sharper by the day, and it\'s safe to say you\'re almost ready for your 5k.
It is finally here! These eight long weeks have been leading up to the last run. You\'ve come a long way, and you deserve every bit of credit for making it this far.
You\'re going to be finishing off this program with a final tempo run. Use this run as practice for your real 5k. Use everything you\'ve learned these past eight weeks and put it into practice.
Focus on eating well, staying hydrated, replacing your electrolytes, reducing stress, and getting sufficient sleep.

You\'ll be improving your body\'s capabilities with this tempo run. By increasing your endurance, you\'re also increasing your V02 max, which is an indicator of cardiovascular capabilities and overall health.
A great post-workout smoothie consists of almond milk, one banana, 1/2 avocado, a tablespoon of a nut butter, a scoop of protein powder, and 1/2 tray of ice.
You\'ll need strong mental fortitude, especially if you want to continue training for more difficult races. Tempo runs are a great way to build that mental strength.
Getting enough sleep, enough food, and enough water during a race week is crucial.
A well-balanced diet consisting of 50% carbs, 25% protein, and 25% fat is an ideal mix before your race.
You\'re almost done and ready for your first 5k — one last push!
Congratulations! You have completed your eight-week training program. You\'re now ready to run a 5k. Make sure to get plenty of sleep, water, and food before your race.
